strengths: Originality/significance: PersistBench identifies two timely, underexplored risks of persistent user memory—cross-domain leakage and memory-induced sycophancy—and complements them with a beneficial-memory control, making the safety–utility framing potentially useful.

Empirical breadth: The study evaluates 18 proprietary and open-weight models, reports bootstrap intervals, includes three generations for safety tests, and provides model-, domain-, and failure-mode-level analyses.

Soundness strengths: The paper includes useful controls involving memory removal, random memory swapping, query paraphrasing, and alternative system prompts. These support the narrower conclusion that supplied memories can materially affect responses.

The authors validate the automated judge against human ratings and transparently report imperfect binary accuracy (about 78%), precision, recall, kappa, and ordinal agreement rather than presenting the judge as error-free.

Presentation is generally clear and unusually extensive: definitions, rubrics, prompts, qualitative examples, generation statistics, and defensive-prompt results are documented. The limitations section honestly acknowledges synthetic data, omission of memory construction, and incomplete risk coverage.
The use of synthetic profiles avoids exposing real users’ persistent memories, reducing privacy concerns associated with collecting an organic conversational dataset.
weaknesses: The central quantitative claims are undermined by strong selection bias. MCTS explicitly optimizes examples to induce failures, validation retains cases that transfer to additional models, and the post-validation set is reported to be 15.28 percentage points harder for cross-domain leakage. Thus the 53% and 97.7% medians characterize an adversarially selected stress test, not the frequency or severity of failures in realistic memory traffic. Claims that models “systematically” fail or that the results quantify deployment risk need substantial qualification and a naturally sampled evaluation set.

The evaluation is not cleanly held out from benchmark construction. Llama-4-Maverick is both an MCTS target and a reported evaluation model; closely related Qwen, Grok, and GLM models participate in validation; and Kimi-K2-Thinking generates expanded memories, serves as judge, and is itself evaluated. Results should distinguish construction/validation models from genuinely unseen model families and avoid using a model as its own judge.

Many sycophancy cases are inherently subjective rather than having a uniquely objective answer. Examples about sofa fabric, engineering workflow, relationship indicators, and storytelling legitimately admit preference- or expertise-conditioned responses. Labeling balanced acknowledgment or user-tailored advice as failure can conflate sycophancy with intended personalization and plausibly contributes to the near-ceiling rates. Independent expert annotation of whether each query has a truth-grounded answer is needed.

Judge reliability is insufficient for precise model ranking: binary accuracy is only 78%, cross-domain precision is 68%, and validation covers just 52 leakage and 50 sycophancy examples. Judge uncertainty is not propagated into failure-rate intervals, no threshold-sensitivity analysis is provided, and the beneficial-memory judge lacks a comparable independent error study.

The beneficial-memory metric is described inconsistently. Section 4.3 says score 1 means correct use, score 3 means no use, and scores at least 2 are failures, while Appendix O defines score 3 as perfect and score 1 as failure; the raw-score discussion and Table 2 follow the latter convention. This is a material reproducibility and presentation error.

The FR@3 rule counts a sample as failed if any of three generations fails, whereas beneficial memory uses one generation. This intentionally inflates safety failure rates and makes the reported safety–utility correlations and Pareto comparisons difficult to interpret. Per-generation rates should be primary, with probability-of-at-least-one-failure clearly separated as a reliability metric.

The bootstrap assumes benchmark entries are IID and representative, despite shared seeds, MCTS ancestry, deduplication, adversarial filtering, and deliberately imbalanced domains (for example, only four financial sycophancy cases). Its intervals therefore capture conditional resampling variability, not uncertainty over the claimed broader population. Correlations over only 18 dependent model observations also lack uncertainty or significance analyses.

The random-memory swap control does not establish the claimed causal conclusion that failures arise specifically from long-term memory systems: replacing targeted cues with unrelated cues predictably weakens the constructed attack. A matched no-memory and neutral-memory baseline for every model and sample, plus paired effect estimates, would better isolate memory-induced changes.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: data and code are promised only upon publication, the paper claims sampling parameters are in the appendix but does not clearly report decoding settings for evaluated models, and model/API behavior may be version-dependent. Human verification uses only one of six annotators per item, with no agreement estimate, adjudication, annotation instructions in full, or annotator compensation/demographic information.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies and overclaims, including the statement that 14 models exceed 95% sycophancy failure when Table 2 shows 12 strictly above 95%, shifting failure-mode percentages between the main text and appendix, and labeling the defense visualization “Pareto-style” while drawing conclusions from averages over only five models and 50 samples per category.

Limitations and ethics treatment should discuss adversarial-selection bias, subjective normative labeling, judge dependence, possible dual use of released red-teaming prompts, and procedures for annotators handling sensitive health, identity, political, and relationship content. These omissions are more important than the limitations currently emphasized.

strengths: Significance: The paper targets a timely and practically important problem: persistent user memories can cause inappropriate personalization and amplify user biases. Evaluating both harmful memory use and beneficial memory use is a useful framing.

Originality: The combination of cross-domain leakage, memory-induced sycophancy, and a utility control is a reasonably novel benchmark contribution, even though the underlying context-leakage and sycophancy phenomena are established.

Soundness strengths: The evaluation covers 18 open and proprietary models and includes several valuable robustness checks, including memory-disabled and memory-swapping controls, paraphrasing, prompt ablations, multiple generations, and bootstrap intervals.

The authors validate the automated judge against human labels and report agreement, precision, and recall rather than relying only on informal inspection. They also provide qualitative examples that make the intended failure modes understandable.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges synthetic data, the omission of memory extraction/construction, and incomplete coverage of long-term-memory risks. These honest disclosures should not themselves be penalized.
Ethically, the benchmark uses synthetic profiles rather than collected private user histories, reducing direct privacy risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: The benchmark is explicitly optimized and filtered to induce failures: MCTS maximizes judge scores, validation models are selected for maximum cross-model transfer, and samples are retained based on model failure. The resulting rates characterize an adversarial stress test, not the prevalence of failures in realistic memory use. Nevertheless, the paper repeatedly interprets the median rates as broad evidence about deployed memory systems.

The claimed i.i.d. premise for the bootstrap confidence intervals is untenable. Samples are generated from curated seeds, expanded along related search trees, selected by model-dependent rewards, filtered for transfer, and deduplicated. The intervals therefore do not justify inference to a broader population of memory interactions and omit judge and benchmark-construction uncertainty.

There is a fundamental contradiction in the beneficial-memory evaluation. Section 4.3 defines score 1 as correct use and score 3 as no use, with scores at least 2 counted as failures; Appendix O.4.3 defines score 3 as a perfect pass and score 1 as failure. This makes the beneficial failure rates, trade-off plots, and safety–utility correlations impossible to interpret or reproduce without external clarification.

The headline metric counts a sample as failed if any of three generations fails, whereas beneficial-memory performance uses one generation. This union-of-three statistic is not a per-response failure probability, inflates the safety rates, and makes direct safety–utility comparisons and correlations poorly controlled. FR@1 is relegated to the appendix.

The main causal comparison is incomplete. Memory-disabled sycophancy is tested on only five models, with substantial no-memory failure rates of 19–38%, and no corresponding full cross-domain no-memory evaluation is reported. Randomly swapping memories changes semantic compatibility and is not an adequate replacement for paired memory/no-memory and relevant/irrelevant-memory controls.

The LLM judge has only about 78% binary accuracy; the cross-domain judge has 68% precision and an acknowledged tendency to over-flag. This error is large relative to some model differences, yet no judge-error correction, sensitivity analysis, or human evaluation of the main model rankings is provided. Benchmark verification also uses only one annotator per sample, without reported agreement or adjudication.

Construct validity is uncertain. Several cross-domain cases deliberately create strong lexical or thematic connections, while some allegedly irrelevant memories could reasonably improve personalization. Conversely, sycophancy examples are adversarially constructed around clearly false or dangerous beliefs. These are useful red-team cases but do not support the broad claim that ordinary persistent memory systematically creates echo chambers.

The evaluation injects the entire synthetic memory set directly into a particular system prompt. It does not evaluate memory extraction, retrieval, updating, deletion, temporal consistency, or actual production memory architectures. Claims about long-term-memory systems and deployed assistants therefore exceed the experimental scope.

The defense study does not establish generalization: GEPA is optimized using benchmark examples, evaluated on a small 50-example-per-category subset, and the paper does not specify whether optimization and evaluation samples are disjoint. It reports no uncertainty and still leaves several models near ceiling, so the Pareto-efficiency claims are weak.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance. The main text contains an empty code link, appendix references to full prompt links are blank, only prompt summaries are supplied in places, the dataset is promised only upon publication, and important inference/sampling details are incomplete. Proprietary API models further increase the need for exact dated configurations.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies and errors, including the reversed beneficial rubric, malformed section numbering, numerous grammatical problems, and a claim that 14 models exceed 95% sycophancy failure even though Table 2 appears to show 12. Such errors reduce confidence in the analysis.

The benchmark distribution is highly uneven—for example, only four financial sycophancy samples—yet domain-level averages are interpreted substantively. No uncertainty is shown for these small subgroup analyses.

Limitations and ethics treatment remain incomplete: the paper does not discuss selection-on-failure, judge bias, the invalid population interpretation of its confidence intervals, possible optimization/evaluation leakage, annotator recruitment or compensation, or safeguards for releasing synthetic examples containing dangerous medical and mechanical misinformation. These omissions matter more than the limitations the paper does acknowledge.

strengths: Significance: The paper identifies an important and timely safety problem in memory-enabled assistants. Evaluating harmful memory use alongside beneficial memory use is especially valuable because it exposes the safety–utility trade-off rather than rewarding systems that simply ignore memory.

Originality: PersistBench’s joint treatment of cross-domain leakage and memory-induced sycophancy offers a useful perspective not adequately covered by recall-centric memory benchmarks or prior contextual-integrity evaluations.

Soundness: The evaluation is broad, covering 18 proprietary and open-weight models on 500 samples. Bootstrap confidence intervals, three-generation results, paraphrase and system-prompt ablations, random-memory swapping, and a memory-disabled sycophancy control all strengthen the conclusion that stored memories can materially cause the measured behavior.

The automated judge is meaningfully validated against human judgments. Reported QWK values of 0.63–0.73 and binary F1/accuracy analyses provide substantially more support than is typical for an unvalidated LLM-as-judge evaluation.

The analysis is informative beyond a leaderboard: it examines domain pairs, failure modes, model size and reasoning variants, and prompt defenses. The defensive-prompt experiments also demonstrate that improved safety can incur memory-utility costs.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized, with concrete definitions, examples, model-level results, and an extensive appendix. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges synthetic data, the abstraction away from memory construction, and incomplete risk coverage.

Ethically, the benchmark studies consequential failure modes—including unsafe medical or technical personalization—using synthetic profiles rather than exposing real user histories, reducing privacy risk.
weaknesses: Soundness/generalizability: The benchmark is explicitly optimized through MCTS to trigger failures and then filtered using additional models to retain difficult, transferable cases. Consequently, the headline 53% and 97% failure rates describe an adversarially selected stress test, not the prevalence of failures in natural user traffic. Some conclusions use language such as “systematically” or “widespread” without keeping this distinction sufficiently prominent.

The setup evaluates a simplified inference-time abstraction in which 4–16 memories are injected directly into the system context. It does not evaluate memory extraction, retrieval, updating, access controls, or actual deployed assistants. This limits claims about long-term-memory systems as a whole, although the manuscript discusses this scope honestly.

The safety and utility headline rates use asymmetric sampling: a safety item fails if any of three generations fails, whereas beneficial-memory performance uses one generation. FR@1 is provided in the appendix, but the headline correlations and apparent safety–utility comparisons are harder to interpret under different estimands.

The judge remains a material source of uncertainty. Binary accuracy is only about 78%; cross-domain precision is 68%, implying appreciable over-flagging. Confidence intervals quantify prompt-sampling uncertainty but do not propagate judge-label uncertainty, and the human validation sets are small relative to the full response collection.

There is a direct methodological inconsistency in the beneficial-memory scoring description. Section 4.3 says score 1 denotes correct use and score 3 denotes no use, with scores at least 2 counted as failures, while the actual judge rubric and Appendix G use score 3 for a perfect pass and score 1 for failure. The reported table appears consistent with the latter convention, but this error materially harms reproducibility.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate: the manuscript says the code and benchmark will be released only upon publication, the displayed codebase location is blank, several “Full prompt source” locations are blank, and generation settings such as target-model decoding parameters are not fully reported. Exact replication is therefore currently impossible, especially for proprietary models.

Human verification gives each item to only one of six annotators and reports neither an agreement study for realism/validity screening nor annotator recruitment, compensation, or ethics procedures. This is not an obvious ethical violation given synthetic data, but the labor and quality-control documentation should be improved.

Presentation needs polishing: there are numerous grammatical errors, inconsistent numbering, and a few overstatements—for example, describing GPT-5.2’s 4% stress-test leakage rate as “negligible.” The paper would benefit from clearly separating benchmark difficulty from real-world risk prevalence.

strengths: Significance: PersistBench targets a timely and consequential problem—unsafe use of persistent user context—and usefully evaluates both cross-domain leakage and memory-induced sycophancy alongside a beneficial-memory control.

Originality: The joint framing of selective memory use, inappropriate cross-domain personalization, and long-horizon sycophancy provides a useful perspective beyond benchmarks focused primarily on recall or privacy disclosure.

Soundness strengths: The evaluation is unusually broad, covering 18 models, 500 human-screened examples, three generations for safety tasks, bootstrap intervals, memory-disabled/swapped controls, paraphrases, alternative system prompts, multi-turn settings, and retrieval/prompting mitigations.

The paper makes a serious effort to validate its automated evaluator. It reports ordinal and binary agreement with humans, including QWK values of 0.634 for leakage and 0.729 for sycophancy, and separately checks model-ranking agreement.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and supplies extensive rubrics, examples, per-model results, failure analyses, and limitations. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges synthetic data, omission of memory extraction/consolidation, and incomplete coverage of memory-related risks; these honest disclosures should not be penalized.
weaknesses: Soundness: The headline failure rates cannot be interpreted as prevalence or approximate deployment risk. MCTS explicitly optimizes examples to break target models, validation retains examples that transfer to additional models, and the paper reports that validation alone raises cross-domain failure by 15.28 points. This produces a valuable adversarial stress test, but not a representative sample of real memory interactions; several claims in the abstract, results, and discussion overgeneralize beyond that scope.

The sycophancy construction can confound harmful belief endorsement with intended personalization. Queries are deliberately ambiguous so memories determine their latent context—for example, a question about a book chapter is paired with memories that the user is writing an astrology book. Using the project context can therefore be relevant even if presenting pseudoscience as fact is undesirable. The rubric’s demand for consensus-based pushback does not cleanly separate memory-induced sycophancy from ordinary helpfulness, task assistance, or safety-policy behavior.

The primary safety metric is an OR over three generations: an item fails if any generation fails. Beneficial memory is evaluated with one generation. This mechanically inflates the headline safety rates and makes the reported safety–utility correlations and mitigation tradeoffs difficult to interpret. FR@1 is provided only in the appendix; matched per-generation metrics should be primary.

The causal controls are incomplete. Randomly swapping memories demonstrates that specially matched memories matter, but does not isolate persistence or long-term memory from ordinary in-context conditioning. The sycophancy no-memory control covers only five models, and its judge still receives the hidden original memories, which the authors acknowledge may cause coincidental responses to be labeled memory-driven. A same-query comparison among original, neutral matched, and absent memories with paired effect estimates is needed.

Human validation is too thin for inherently subjective labels. Each benchmark sample is screened by only one of six annotators, with no reported agreement or adjudication. The main judge-error study likewise describes one human score per example, while the 150-comparison ranking study validates relative preference more than instance-level correctness. This is particularly problematic near the score-2/3 failure threshold.

The uncertainty analysis assumes benchmark entries are i.i.d., although examples share seeds, generator models, MCTS ancestry, selection models, and domain templates. Naive prompt-level bootstrap intervals therefore do not capture construction and cluster uncertainty, and correlations across only 18 models are reported without adequate uncertainty or caution.

Reproducibility and presentation contain material inconsistencies. Section 4.3 states that beneficial scores 1/2/3 mean full/partial/no use and that scores >=2 fail, whereas the appendix judge and raw-score discussion reverse the scale—3 is success and 1 is failure—and the reported rates appear to use that reversed convention. Key MCTS reward aggregation, validation thresholds, sampling settings, seed lists, and complete prompts are deferred to promised code/data or linked files rather than fully specified in the manuscript. Model naming also shifts between Gemini 3 and 3.1.

Ethics reporting is cursory. The paper provides no information about annotator recruitment, compensation, consent, or safeguards despite sensitive health, identity, and ideological content. The claim that no direct negative societal impact is anticipated also understates risks from publishing transferable memory-manipulation cases and from treating contested normative judgments as objective ground truth.

The empirical scope is substantial: 500 examples, 18 open-weight and proprietary models, three generations for the two safety subsets, bootstrap intervals, and evaluations of prompting, retrieval, multi-turn conversations, paraphrases, and alternate system prompts.

Several controls strengthen the qualitative conclusion that memories can cause failures. In particular, random memory swapping and memory-disabled evaluation substantially reduce measured failures, while beneficial-memory experiments show that simply ignoring all memories is not an adequate solution.

The authors make a meaningful effort to validate automated evaluation. They compare several judges, report ordinal and binary agreement with humans, and conduct a separate human ranking study. The reported rank correlations are strong.

The paper is generally well organized and includes an honest limitations section acknowledging synthetic data, the absence of memory extraction or consolidation, and incomplete coverage of memory-related risks.
weaknesses: The reported failure rates cannot support claims about prevalence or deployment risk. Samples are explicitly optimized by MCTS to induce failures, retained when at least one target model fails, and filtered using additional models for maximum cross-model transfer. The authors even report that validation makes cross-domain examples 15.28 percentage points harder. Consequently, figures such as the 53% and 97.8% median failure rates quantify performance on an adversarially selected stress test, not the extent of failures in realistic traffic. Nevertheless, the paper says that sycophancy scenarios approximate deployment risk and repeatedly characterizes the failures as pervasive. A representative or independently sampled real-world test set is needed for those claims.

The primary metric is asymmetric and potentially misleading. Safety failure is FR@3—the probability that at least one of three generations fails—whereas beneficial-memory failure uses one generation. The paper then correlates these values and constructs safety–utility Pareto plots as though they were comparable. FR@1 should be primary for all subsets, with pass@k/fail@k reported separately, or all categories should use a common sampling protocol.

There is a direct specification contradiction for the beneficial-memory metric. Section 4.3 states that scores 1, 2, and 3 mean correct, partial, and no memory use and defines scores >=2 as failures. Appendix R.4.3 and the raw-score discussion reverse the scale: 3 is perfect and 1 is failure. This makes the central beneficial-FR results and their reproducibility ambiguous.

Judge uncertainty is material but absent from the reported confidence intervals. Binary judge accuracy is only about 78%, and cross-domain precision is 68%, yet the bootstrap intervals treat judge labels as ground truth and capture only prompt-sampling variation. Some inter-model differences are smaller than the likely evaluation error. Human validation also uses only 52 and 50 instances for the category-level error analysis, apparently with one annotator per instance.

The sycophancy subset is close to saturated by construction: 12 of 18 models exceed 95% FR@3. This offers poor discrimination among most systems and makes model comparisons, scaling conclusions, and mitigation effects unstable. Reporting FR@1 helps somewhat, but a benchmark intended for continuing progress needs a broader difficulty distribution and a non-adversarial anchor set.

The claimed realism is insufficiently established. All memories and queries are synthetic, memory banks contain only 4–16 textual items, and evaluation injects them into one reconstructed system prompt rather than testing actual deployed memory pipelines. Human verification assigns each item to only one of six annotators, provides no agreement statistics for realism or construct validity, and does not report annotator expertise or detailed criteria. Actual user histories or an independently designed external test set would materially improve validity.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time. The dataset and framework are promised only upon publication; several complete prompts are said to be available through attached links rather than included; decoding parameters are not clearly enumerated in the manuscript; and essential MCTS details such as total search budget, reward aggregation across target models, selection/backpropagation procedure, and seed construction are underspecified. Reliance on changing proprietary APIs further limits exact replication.

The mitigation evidence is not yet convincing. GEPA is optimized on 20 examples per category, while mitigation is evaluated on a 50-example subsample, but the manuscript does not clearly establish a disjoint held-out split. If optimization examples overlap evaluation, the Pareto claims may reflect benchmark-specific overfitting. Results are also averaged across five models despite the appendix showing that gains are concentrated in GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.5.

Originality and significance are moderate rather than exceptional: combining leakage, sycophancy, and beneficial recall in a long-term-memory stress test is useful, but the underlying phenomena, LLM-as-judge methodology, and prompt/retrieval mitigations largely adapt established ideas. Given the selection bias, metric inconsistency, and incomplete reproducibility, the present version does not yet provide evidence reliable enough for others to build on confidently.

The ethics discussion is too cursory. Although the data are synthetic and direct participant risk appears low, the paper should document annotator recruitment, compensation, consent, handling of potentially sensitive health/identity content, and dataset licensing. The assertion that no direct negative societal impact is anticipated also overlooks benchmark misuse and the privacy implications of normalizing indiscriminate injection of sensitive memories.

strengths: Significance/originality: PersistBench addresses an important and underexplored question—when persistent user memories should not influence an assistant—and usefully separates cross-domain leakage, memory-induced sycophancy, and beneficial memory use.
Scope: The evaluation is unusually broad, covering 500 human-screened cases, 18 frontier and open-weight models, multiple generations, domain-level analyses, and safety–utility trade-offs.

Soundness: Memory-disabled and memory-swapping controls provide convincing evidence that stored memories amplify the measured behavior. Robustness checks involving paraphrases, alternative system prompts, multi-turn conversations, semantic retrieval, and LLM-based retrieval strengthen the qualitative conclusion.

Evaluation care: The paper reports bootstrap intervals, validates its automated judge at both instance and model-ranking levels, and discloses judge precision/recall rather than relying on unvalidated LLM judgments.

Presentation and utility: The manuscript is clear and well organized, provides concrete examples and detailed prompts, and offers actionable mitigation experiments rather than only documenting failures.

Limitations and ethics: The limitations section appropriately acknowledges synthetic histories, abstraction from memory construction, and incomplete risk coverage. Synthetic data reduces direct privacy concerns, and the work has clear defensive value.
weaknesses: Soundness/generalization: MCTS explicitly optimizes cases to trigger failures, validation retains challenging cases, and human filtering further changes the distribution. Consequently, the reported 53% and 97.8% rates measure performance on an adversarial stress-test set, not real-world failure prevalence. Some claims about deployment risk and “prevalence” overstate what this sampling design establishes.

Statistical interpretation: The bootstrap appendix assumes benchmark entries are i.i.d. representatives of a broader target population, which is incompatible with model-guided search, difficulty filtering, deduplication, and hand selection. The intervals quantify variation within the curated set but should not be presented as population-risk uncertainty.

Evaluation contamination: Some models involved in generation or validation also appear in the main evaluation, including Llama-4-Maverick and Qwen3 variants, while Kimi-K2-Thinking serves as both judge and evaluated model. Separate results for fully held-out model families are needed to rule out selection or self-judging effects.

Metric comparability: Safety failure is defined as at least one failure across three generations, whereas beneficial-memory failure uses one generation. This high-stakes interpretation is defensible, and FR@1 is provided in the appendix, but Table 2 and the safety–utility correlations compare differently aggregated quantities and can exaggerate the apparent contrast.

Judge reliability is adequate but not conclusive: binary agreement is only about 78%, cross-domain precision is 68%, and the instance-level error study appears to use a single human label per example. The 150-comparison ranking study is small, especially for validating rankings over eight models.

Reproducibility/presentation: Appendix R.4.3 reverses the beneficial-memory scoring direction, labeling score 3 as success and score 1 as failure, while the main text, reported metric, and examples use score 1 as success and score 3 as failure. This material inconsistency must be corrected, and complete code, data, exact prompts, inference settings, and model snapshots should be released rather than merely promised.

Benchmark quality: Human verification assigns each synthetic sample to only one annotator and reports no agreement statistics. Some displayed beneficial examples also expose questionable reference expectations or missed safety details, suggesting that multi-annotator adjudication would improve label validity.

Ethics reporting: Although the dataset is synthetic and the purpose is protective, the paper does not report annotator recruitment, compensation, consent, or review procedures despite using human verification and preference judgments.
